blocks.text: A function names a transformation from parameters to a return value. Scope limits accessible names; a pure function depends only on arguments and changes no outside state, making output predictable. Always separate the intention, the incoming data, the transformation being performed, and the observable result. A function names a transformation from parameters to a return value. Scope limits accessible names; a pure function depends only on arguments and changes no outside state, making output predictable. Read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. This habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding.

Arguments are evaluated and bound to local parameters; return ends the call. Closures retain lexical environment, but hidden mutable dependencies complicate tests. In a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or DevTools instead of assuming it works. Observable evidence is more reliable than intuition.

blocks.text: An array orders values; each method expresses a collection intention. filter selects, map transforms one-to-one, find locates one item, some/every answer questions, and reduce aggregates. An array orders values; each method expresses a collection intention. filter selects, map transforms one-to-one, find locates one item, some/every answer questions, and reduce aggregates. Read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. This habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding.

blocks.text: An object maps keys to values and often represents an entity. Spread creates a shallow copy; every changed nested branch must also be copied to preserve the old version. Always separate the intention, the incoming data, the transformation being performed, and the observable result. This separation lets you predict behavior before running code and diagnose an error precisely.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: Revising a form while keeping the original requires a new sheet and a separate copy of every changed attachment.

An object maps keys to values and often represents an entity. Spread creates a shallow copy; every changed nested branch must also be copied to preserve the old version. Read the example from top to bottom, identify every input, and predict the output before running the command. This habit turns memorized syntax into reusable understanding.

Destructuring reads named properties; rest collects others. ...object copies first-level references, not nested objects, and spread order decides which value wins. In a real project, verify this mechanism with the browser, terminal, or DevTools instead of assuming it works. Observable evidence is more reliable than intuition.

Return a new object for every update, copy only the touched nested path, and use Object.is to verify unchanged branches remain shared. Finally apply the concept through one small isolated change, check the result, and revert if needed. Short changes make cause and effect easy to connect.
